summary: Alarmed by the raising of Lazarus, the council plots Jesus’ death; Caiaphas says one man should die for the people, and Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.
key_insight: Caiaphas meant a political calculation: better that one man die than that the whole nation perish. John says God spoke through him anyway. Jesus would die for the nation, and not for that nation only, but to gather into one the scattered children of God.
story: News of Lazarus reached the leaders in Jerusalem. The chief priests and the Pharisees called the council together and asked, “What shall we do? For this Man works many signs. If we let Him alone like this, everyone will believe in Him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation.”

Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, cut them off: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and not that the whole nation should perish.”

He did not say this on his own authority. Being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for that nation only, but also to gather together in one the children of God who were scattered abroad. From that day on, they plotted to put Jesus to death.
So Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews. He went away to the country near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stayed there with His disciples.

scene.label: The council
scene.text: The Sanhedrin was the highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, led by the high priest. Its chief priests, mostly Sadducees, and its Pharisees often disagreed with each other, but here they act together.

scene.label: Caiaphas
scene.text: Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, longer than anyone else under Roman rule, and he was the son-in-law of Annas (John 18:13). In 1990 a family burial box inscribed with the name Caiaphas was found in Jerusalem, probably from his family’s tomb.

scene.label: “Our place and nation”
scene.text: “Place” probably meant the temple, and “nation” the limited self-rule Rome allowed. Rome kept order through these leaders, and unrest could cost them both. About forty years later, Rome did destroy the temple.

scene.label: A high priest’s prophecy
scene.text: In Israel’s early history the high priest sought God’s answers through the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21). John sees God speaking through the office, even when the man who held it meant something else.

scene.label: Ephraim
scene.text: A town at the edge of the wilderness north of Jerusalem, probably the village now called et-Taiyibeh, near Bethel and some fifteen miles from the city (compare 2 Chronicles 13:19).

witnesses.john: Only John records this council. It shows that the raising of Lazarus, Jesus’ last sign before the cross, became the immediate cause of Jesus’ death. John adds his own comment on Caiaphas, hearing in a cynical plan a true prophecy of Jesus dying for others, and he widens it to God’s scattered children, echoing Jesus’ “other sheep” (10:16).

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ enemies decide on His death, but God has already decided its meaning: one Man dying in the place of the people, to gather God’s scattered children into one family.
seeing.living: The council feared losing its place, so it chose to lose Jesus instead. When Jesus becomes inconvenient, be honest about what you are protecting. And take courage: no plot against Christ is beyond God’s power to turn toward His saving purpose.
seeing.ponder: What “place” of your own would you be tempted to protect, even at the cost of Jesus?

preaching.big_idea: Caiaphas planned one death to save a nation; God meant that death to gather His scattered children.
outline: A council afraid of losing its place (47–48)
A plan for one man to die (49–50)
A prophecy greater than the speaker (51–52)
A plot set and a Savior withdrawn (53–54)
preaching.watch_for: John recalls Caiaphas’s words, “one man should die for the people,” in John 18:14, just as Jesus is brought under arrest to the high priest’s house. The trial is meant to be read in their light.

title: The Council Plots His Death
